newsitem.title: USA: Clinton appeals for unity, votes.
newsitem.headline: Clinton appeals for unity, votes.

text.p: President Bill Clinton worshipped at a black church on Sunday and began his sprint to the campaign finish line with a sermon-like appeal for reconciliation, unity and votes.

"We will never be what we ought to be if we allow our country to be led by those who believe we are better off on our own, and who seek to pursue that path by driving wedges between us and exploiting our fears and convincing us that our brothers and sisters of different races, different faiths, different walks of life, are our inherent enemies," he said.
"That is a prescription for disaster," Clinton said from the pulpit of St. Paul's African Episcopal Methodist Church, where civil rights leader Martin Luther King once spoke.

After the pastor, the Rev. Leroy Washington Jr., introduced him with a plea to the congregation to vote on Tuesday, Clinton said, "I know I'm preaching to the choir today, but in the next two days we need the choir to preach."
Clinton later addressed a rally in West Palm Beach, Florida, before heading north for a non-stop day of appearances in New Jersey, Massachusetts and Maine.

With Election Day so near and most opinion polls showing him with a commanding lead over Republican rival Bob Dole, Clinton has been delivering a pointed message cloaked in lofty themes as he reaches out to voters across the country.
While Dole was criss-crossing the country attacking Clinton, the president sounded more like a Sunday school teacher, quoting from the Bible as he preached about the need for tolerance in America.

"We know that there are still too many white people who wouldn't feel as comfortable as I do sitting in this church," Clinton told the black congregation. "They read the same Bible you do. They claim the same saviour you do. They ought to feel at home here."
The church where he spoke was across Tampa Bay from St. Petersburg -- a community torn by racial rioting last month.

After the service, Clinton met with St. Petersburg Mayor David Fischer and discussed the death of 18-year-old Tyron Lewis, a black who was shot and killed by a white police officer who stopped him for speeding.
The incident touched off rioting and has prompted the NAACP and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference to call for an investigation by outside authorities.
White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton and Fischer discussed ways the federal government could work to ease the economic problems of the city, which have contributed to the tensions.
Clinton mentioned the incident only in passing, but quoted President Abraham Lincoln's warning that "a house divided against itself cannot stand."
He said the choice before the voters on Tuesday was whether to build the nation's future on the "shifting sands of division or the strong rock of common ground."
"I don't think anybody should have a guarantee, but I think everybody should have a chance," Clinton said.

Although polling conducted for Reuters shows Clinton's lead over Dole narrowing, Clinton campaign officials insisted their extensive polling shows the incumbent with a steady 12 to 15 percentage point lead.
The proof of their confidence can be seen in the states where Clinton has chosen to take his message during the final days before Tuesday's election.

Four years ago Clinton ignored Florida as a lost cause, but this year he and Vice President Al Gore have targeted the state -- convinced they can become the first Democratic ticket to win there since Jimmy Carter and Walter Mondale in 1976.
